name: Gareth Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. This is all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior with a contractor that does the electrics on a big new-build housing estate, about three hundred houses going up on the edge of town. Every house is near enough identical, so I do first fix all day: back boxes, cable runs through the studs, the consumer unit position. I'm on a price per plot, so if I'm quick, I earn well. My supervisor Clive checks my plots, and he still finds the odd cable I've nicked with the staple gun.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm, and the money, honestly, I'm on more than most juniors because of the price work. What wears me out is the mud and the 6am starts in winter. I married Hannah last year, she's a receptionist at the dentist, and we've got a good deposit saved, nearly a year of wages, from both of us living with her parents for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with building houses. At church I'd say hard work's still worth something. Online I wouldn't bother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. Houses still need building and I'm getting faster. Three hundred houses on one estate means three hundred kitchens that still need a lad with a staple gun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my licence, keep doing price work, and buy our first house next spring, maybe on this estate with the staff discount. Keep putting money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like things are on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything worrying you even when nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing slowdowns. If interest rates go up, the builder stops building, and the price work dries up overnight. It happened to Clive in 2008, he told me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the estate stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move to a domestic firm, there are plenty round here. Less money than price work, but steady. And we'd have the deposit to fall back on.

At church I'd say **hard work** is still worth something.
think: Houses still need building and I'm **getting faster** every month.
Every new kitchen still needs **a lad** with a staple gun.
do: Get my **licence** and keep doing price work.
Buy our **first house** next spring with the staff discount.
S0.quote: Three hundred houses on one estate means three hundred kitchens that still need a lad with a staple gun.
fieldNote: His real exposure is to the **housing cycle**, not AI.
Price work makes him **well-paid** for a junior.
Remembers his supervisor's **2008** story as a warning.

steps.text: Buy a first house on the estate next spring
Keep doing first fix on price work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mainly office stuff and builders will always need sparks. At church I'd say look after your family and stay useful. To my mates I'd say watch the factory side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, new-build is where they'd try robots and factory kit first. They already send pre-wired looms for some houses. If the factory sends the houses pre-wired, there's nothing left for a first-fix lad like me to do on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get licensed, then move off pure first fix into second fix and testing. Learn the design software Clive's starting to use, once he says it's worth it. Buy the house, but a bit cheaper than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine for now, but I can see where it's heading on estates like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older lads who only do first fix and don't want to learn anything else. Dave's 54 and he's been stapling cable for thirty years. He'd struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a cheaper house. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the price work might not last. A smaller mortgage means we're fine even on a normal domestic wage. Hannah's dad said the same, and he's usually right.

**Pre-wired** houses would leave nothing for a first-fix lad.
do: Move from first fix into **second fix and testing**.
Learn Clive's **design software** once he vouches for it.
feel: **Uneasy**, seeing where estate work is heading.

fieldNote: He spots that his specific work, **first fix on estates**, is the most repeatable.
Takes advice from **family elders** on money.
Steady adopter: waits for his **supervisor** to try tools first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too fast and businesses need to keep apprentices on. I'd vote for whoever backs trades and families. At church we'd talk about looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. The site office goes in 2028, then around 2031 robots can do what I do on an estate easier than anywhere. I'd be 32. A robot would find an estate of identical houses easier than any job I've ever done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get licensed fast. Move to a domestic firm doing old houses within a year, where robots would struggle longer. Buy a small house with a small mortgage, not the big one. Keep a year's wages in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have savings and a trade, but the work I'm good at would go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hannah decide about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want them, that wouldn't change. Maybe we'd wait a year to see how the money goes. Hannah's mum would help with childcare, that's what family's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With three years before the robots, what's your plan for those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Earn as much as I can on price work for one more year, then switch to domestic. Build up a name with customers in older houses. People in those houses want a man they know, not a machine.

I'd be **32** when the work I'm good at goes.

S2.quote: A robot would find an estate of identical houses easier than any job I've ever done.
fieldNote: Expects his **estate first-fix work** to vanish but has savings and other options.
Sees **older houses** as the safer niche.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty to get ready if you're willing to work. I'd tell younger lads to learn more than one part of the job. At church I'd be steady about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm all right if I move now. Robots come around 2034, when I'm 35, and by then I'd want to be a qualified tester or running small jobs. Five years is enough to stop being a first-fix lad and become the man who signs the certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence first, then the inspection qualification within three years. Move to domestic and small commercial work. Buy the house. Start a family in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It's like seeing a hill coming on a long drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider starting your own small firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, with Hannah doing the books. It'd be a risk, but a small local firm with a good name lasts. I'd want a couple of years at a domestic firm first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dave, the older lad on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mate Dave to do the inspection course too, he's got the hands. He'd probably say he'll retire first. He might be right.

I'd tell younger lads to learn **more than one part** of the job.

fieldNote: More warning lets him **move up** from repetitive work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there's no excuse for not getting ready. At work I'd tell apprentices to aim higher than first fix. At church I'd be calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. By 2039 I'd be 40, maybe running my own small firm with a couple of lads. Ten years is long enough for me to go from stapling cable to running my own firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Licence, inspection ticket, a few years at a domestic firm, then my own firm with Hannah. Buy a house, have kids. Use AI for quoting once it's normal in the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, even. It's a proper run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children follow you into the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they wanted to, yes, but I'd push them to learn the testing and design side too. Robots in 2039 would mean they'd need more than hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A housing crash, same as always. That's the risk that's been there all along. AI wouldn't change that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because estate work like mine would go first. What'd help is firms being made to keep apprentices on and cheap courses for testing and inspection. I'd rather earn a smaller wage doing a real job than be paid to sit at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about housing. If robots build houses cheaper, maybe my kids could actually afford one. That's the one good thing I can see.

headlineQuote: I'd rather earn a smaller wage doing a real job than be paid to sit at home.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old junior** doing first fix on a new-build estate, well paid on price work.
Recently married, he and Hannah have nearly **a year's wages** saved for a deposit.
He knows **repetitive estate work** is where robots come first, so AGI by 2028 makes him anxious.
With more time he plans to become a **tester** and start his own firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **estate first-fix** work would be the first to go.
